description: We are a team of students from the Department of Artificial Intelligence at the Institute of Applied Systems Analysis (IASA), Kyiv Polytechnic Institute (KPI). We combine mathematical thinking, programming skills, and creativity to tackle complex challenges. We're here to push boundaries, build something extraordinary, and prove what IASA students are capable of.
summary: My Moon Base is a free browser game for kids aged 7–12, built for the "Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge. The player is the chief engineer of the first base at the Moon's south pole: they launch cargo from Earth, build modules with robots, explore ice craters and look after a crew of four specialists. Solar panels give only a few power blocks, so every choice has a cost: more power for life support means more oxygen but slower robots; a greenhouse gives food but drinks water; a shelter protects the crew from radiation but needs power exactly when a solar storm comes. The storms are real 2024 events from NASA DONKI, and today's space weather is fetched live. Every evening a short report explains what changed and why, so kids learn cause and effect, not just numbers. Three short chapters add the trade-offs step by step: power and oxygen, then ice, food and science, then radiation and health. This matters because space agencies are planning real bases near the Moon's south pole, and today's kids may become their crews. The game runs in any desktop browser, in English and Ukrainian.
details:
What it does

My Moon Base is a browser game for kids aged 7 to 12. You play the chief engineer of the first base at the Moon’s south pole, the same area NASA plans to explore with Artemis. You walk your engineer around the base and out onto the surface with W A S D, and you run the base from a tablet. The game pauses whenever the tablet is open, because we didn’t want kids to feel rushed while they think.

A game day lasts about three minutes. First you pack a rocket on Earth. More cargo means more fuel, and the fuel is heavy too. A traffic light tells you how risky the launch is. Once you land, the real puzzle starts. The solar panels give you only a few blocks of power, and you have to split them between life support, the greenhouse, the antenna, the shelter, the lab, the medbay and the robots. There’s never enough for everything. Oxygen is made from water and power, water comes from ice that your geologist digs out of dark craters, and the greenhouse needs both water and power to grow food. Robots build new modules and can bury them under Moon soil to block radiation. They never get a radiation dose, but they use power. Your four astronauts get hungry, can get sick and slowly collect radiation, especially when they work outside.

Then a solar storm warning arrives. These storms are real events from NASA’s DONKI database, so the warning shows the actual date and flare class. You have a few hours to get everyone inside and give the shelter enough power. At the end of each day the base gives you a short report about what changed and why. We think that report is the most important part of the game, because it turns “my oxygen went down” into “my oxygen went down because I took power away from life support.”

The game has three chapters of about 25 minutes each. The first is about landing, power and oxygen. The second adds ice, food and supply ships. In the third you have to survive the real solar storms of May 2024. There is also a “Demo for judges” button that shows everything in about five minutes.

Why it matters

We wanted kids to feel the trade-offs real mission engineers deal with, not just read about them. Nobody tells you the right answer in this game. You find out the next morning whether your choice worked. The game is free, runs in a normal browser without installing anything, and is in English and Ukrainian. Any classroom or family can just open it and play.

NASA data we used

The storms come from 15 real 2024 events in NASA DONKI, and we checked every one against the DONKI API. The start screen also pulls the last week of space weather live from DONKI and labels it LIVE. If you’re offline, it shows our saved data and labels it ARCHIVE. Radiation doses are based on the typical ISS dose from NASA OSDR / RadLab (about 0.5 mSv a day) and the 600 mSv career limit from NASA-STD-3001. We sped time up so kids can see the effect in minutes, and the game says so. Short health facts come from NASA OSDR, the terrain is based on NASA Moon Trek, and the greenhouse uses the Canadian Space Agency’s material on growing plants in space.

How we built it

Engine and language: Unity 6.6 (URP), written in C# and exported to WebGL so it runs in the browser.

Interface: UI Toolkit.

Data: game balance, texts and NASA data all live in JSON files, so we could tune numbers without touching code.

Live data: the DONKI API.

Testing: the core logic has automated tests.

Teamwork: GitHub, with a branch and pull request for every task.

Sound: we generated the sound effects in code instead of downloading them.

AI: Claude helped us write code and kid-friendly texts, and some sprites were made with OpenAI image generation. Every AI-assisted file is marked in the repository.

Hardware: our own laptops.

What we think is creative

Our favourite part is that the danger is real. A kid can say “this storm actually happened on 10 May 2024”, and that’s true. We also liked mixing a walking world with a management game. When you send your geologist to a far crater, you see them walk there and you watch the radiation bar fill up. Robots versus people also became a real choice: robots cost power, people cost radiation. And when you step into a module, its roof disappears and the outside gets darker, which makes the base feel like a place and not a spreadsheet.

What we kept in mind

Most of our team are beginners, and we had one weekend. So we chose three chapters that work over five that don’t. For 7 to 12-year-olds we kept every text short, explained every space word, added a helper line that suggests what to do next, and made sure nobody dies. The worst that can happen is that your crew has to fly home. We used only real NASA numbers with sources and dates, we’re honest about what we simplified, and the game has no NASA logos or mission emblems.
